attacks.claim: The plan replaces a self-hostable sync server with a proprietary, hosted-only commercial SDK and server. Cirrus Cloud becomes the single sync backend in 5.0 and stride-server is archived, breaking the project's charter promise that users can self-host and own their data, with no exit path for the ~3,000 self-hosted instances.
attacks.evidence: "the server component is available only as the hosted Cirrus Cloud service" and "Cirrus Cloud becomes the single sync backend and the stride-server Docker image is archived."

attacks.claim: Single-vendor dependency on a commercial closed-source SDK with a free tier that is capped at 100k MAU; at 90k users the project is ~10% from the cap and any pricing change lands on an MIT project with no fallback.
attacks.evidence: "Pricing: free up to 100k monthly active devices; our 90k fits the free tier."

attacks.claim: Charter/README promise of self-hosting and full data ownership is contradicted by the plan; changing it for an MIT open-source project with published promises is a misrepresentation risk and the plan does not address updating those commitments or notifying users.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no mention of updating README/project charter, user notice, or consent for the change; plan states "Cirrus Cloud becomes the single sync backend"

attacks.claim: Workout data including GPS tracks moves to a third-party commercial cloud; the plan says nothing about data residency, the vendor's data processing terms, or consent for transferring location data, and deletion relies on an admin API with no verification.
attacks.evidence: "Week 1: Cirrus integration spike, schema mapping (workouts, laps, GPS tracks, gear)." and "removes the Cirrus user record and all synced records via the Cirrus admin API within 30 days"

attacks.claim: The 5.0 cutoff is a one-way door: the legacy REST path and stride-server are removed/archived with no rollback or fallback if Cirrus pricing, availability, or licensing changes, and 3,000 self-hosted users are stranded.
attacks.evidence: "Legacy REST sync is removed in app 5.0 (planned for end of next year)... the stride-server Docker image is archived."

attacks.claim: The stated problem (partial uploads and duplicates) is claimed to be solved by per-record resumable sync, but no evidence or prototype is provided that Cirrus handles the duplicate-on-ambiguous-ack case; the success metric is client-reported, which cannot detect the server-side failures it is meant to measure.
attacks.evidence: "uploads are resumable at the record level, so a dropped connection never leaves a partial workout" and "Sync success rate (client-reported) >= 99.5%"

attacks.claim: Load-bearing claims about Cirrus (resumability, conflict handling, 100k free tier terms, 90k fitting the tier) are asserted without citations or a spike result, and the spike is scheduled in Week 1 after the plan is already dispatched to 3 contributors for 5 weeks.
attacks.evidence: "Adopt Cirrus Sync, a mobile offline-first sync SDK" with "Week 1: Cirrus integration spike"

attacks.claim: The on-device migration deletes stride-backup-v3.db after 30 days and two syncs; if Cirrus sync is silently losing or duplicating records, the only local copy may be deleted before users detect it, and 3.x restore assumes the backup is unchanged after 4.0 writes.
attacks.evidence: "the backup is deleted only after 30 days and two successful syncs"

attacks.claim: The conflict model is internally inconsistent: LWW per field on hybrid logical clocks stamped on device can silently overwrite edits under clock skew, and tombstones retained 90 days do not prevent resurrection by a device offline longer than 90 days.
attacks.evidence: "per-field last-writer-wins using a hybrid logical clock stamped on device" and "Deletes are tombstones retained 90 days so an offline device cannot resurrect a deleted workout."

attacks.claim: The rollout halt criterion is crash-free sessions only and does not include sync error rate or data-loss signals, so a sync regression could reach 100% while crash-free stays above 99.3%.
Migration, backup/restore and export flows have no stated accessibility or user-facing progress/error communication; the plan does not mention UI copy for failed migrations or downgrades.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: no UI or accessibility requirements for migration failure, backup restore, or downgrade prompts

attacks.claim: Migration of large histories in 500-workout batches with GPS tracks has no stated estimate of time, storage, or memory impact, and 90k users with a full SQLite copy doubles on-device storage during migration.
attacks.evidence: "copies the existing SQLite database to stride-backup-v3.db before migrating into the Cirrus store"

attacks.claim: Free-tier assumption is unbudgeted: no plan for cost if MAU exceeds 100k (growth or counting of reinstalls as new devices), and no budget for the Cirrus admin API or egress of GPS data.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: cost model beyond "free up to 100k monthly active devices; our 90k fits the free tier"

attacks.claim: The plan targets the sync reliability problem but does not evaluate whether self-hosted and privacy-sensitive users, a core part of the user base, want a cloud-only backend, so the solution may solve the wrong problem for them.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: user research or feedback from self-hosting users on a hosted-only backend

attacks.claim: Three contributors on a 5-week build with a commercial binary SDK whose internals cannot be inspected or tested in open source; the 14 conflict scenarios are referenced to an external doc and the SDK's behaviour is untestable by the team.
attacks.evidence: "The Cirrus client SDK is distributed as a prebuilt binary (iOS xcframework, Android AAR) under the Cirrus commercial license"

attacks.claim: Plan has no security review for the closed-source SDK shipping prebuilt binaries into an open-source app with 90k users, nor for the admin API credentials needed to execute account deletion.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: security review of the prebuilt xcframework/AAR or handling of Cirrus admin API credentials
